lesson.title: How Often Things Go Wrong: Quantifying the Bit Error Rate
lesson.summary: Bit error rate is the fraction of transmitted bits that arrive flipped, and it is the crucial link between physical layer conditions like noise and interference and the packet loss that higher layers actually experience.
lesson.body:
Attenuation weakens a signal, and noise and interference corrupt it, but a network engineer eventually needs a single number that summarizes how badly a link is actually performing. That number is the bit error rate, or BER: the fraction of transmitted bits that arrive flipped, that is, a 0 that was read as a 1 or a 1 that was read as a 0. A BER of 10 to the negative 6 means, on average, one bit out of every million is received incorrectly. BER is a property of the physical link and its conditions, distance, SNR, modulation scheme, rather than a property of any particular file or message, though its consequences show up wherever bits happen to travel.

To see why this matters in practice, take a link with a BER of 10 to the negative 6 and send a 1 megabyte file, which is 8,000,000 bits. The expected number of corrupted bits is simply 8,000,000 multiplied by 0.000001, or 8 bit errors across the whole file. Eight flipped bits sounds small next to eight million transmitted bits, but where those errors land matters enormously, because data does not travel as one continuous stream from the application's point of view. It travels in discrete chunks handed to lower layers as frames or packets.

This is where BER connects directly to packet loss. Consider a typical 1500 byte packet, which is 12,000 bits. Using the same BER of 10 to the negative 6, and the fact that for a small per bit error probability the chance of at least one error in n bits is approximately n times that probability, the chance that this particular packet contains at least one bit error is roughly 12,000 times 0.000001, or about 0.012, meaning roughly 1.2 percent of packets on this link will contain an error somewhere inside them. Since most protocols detect a corrupted packet using a checksum or CRC and simply discard it rather than trying to guess which bits are wrong, that 1.2 percent of damaged packets becomes, functionally, 1.2 percent packet loss, even though the underlying physical link never dropped a single bit outright. It just delivered some of them wrong, which downstream layers treat as equivalent to not delivering them at all.

This relationship is also why BER requirements get dramatically stricter as packets get larger or as links get faster. A gigabit Ethernet link pushing far more bits per second through the same BER would produce proportionally more corrupted packets per second unless the underlying physical layer is engineered for a much lower BER in the first place, which is exactly why wired Ethernet standards typically target a BER many orders of magnitude better than 10 to the negative 6, often specified around 10 to the negative 10 or better, while a noisy wireless link may operate acceptably at a BER several orders of magnitude worse. Bit error rate is, in short, the bridge between the physical world of attenuation, noise, and interference, and the practical, everyday experience of packet loss that every layer above the physical layer has to cope with.
